https://business-review.eu/lifestyle/br-.text: BR Exclusive | architect Eliza Yokina: “Architecture can offer a sense of comfort, belonging, and identity” How can architecture shape the way we encounter an artist’s universe without competing with the works themselves? This question lies at the heart of Transylvania | Extravaganza , the largest exhibition dedicated to Romanian painter Ștefan Câlția, bringing together more than 80 works from different stages of his career. Curated by Liviana Dan, the exhibition unfolds inside the former Ursuline pedagogical school in Sibiu, a historic building whose classrooms, vaults, and courtyards become part of the visitor’s journey. Architect Eliza Yokina, founding partner of Cumulus Architecture, translated the curatorial vision into a restrained, minimally invasive exhibition design that allows Câlția’s poetic world to enter into dialogue with the architecture and history of the Ursuline complex. In this interview, she discusses her first encounter with the artist, the relationship between space, memory and heritage, and the architectural decisions that transform the exhibition from a sequence of artworks into an immersive journey. What is the first image, feeling, or idea that comes to mind when you think of Ștefan Câlția’s artistic universe? I’m thinking of the most distinctive colour found on a house in Sona and so beautifully told by Stafan Câlția in a film made by Diana Iabrasu: “The Blue Left Among Us.” Imagine you’re speaking to someone who has never heard of Ștefan Câlția and has never visited Romania. How would you describe his work in a single paragraph? Read more about Last chance to enter Ștefan Câlția’s Transylvanian universe as Transilvania | Extravaganza enters its final week read more Ștefan Câlția’s art is deeply connected to a world that defines us—one that, most of the time, remains hidden from view (though not from our gaze). He successfully reveals this floating essence through deeply inspiring storytelling. His paintings depict a village life and architecture that still exist today, capturing the harmonious identity shared between nature and spaces shaped by humanity. This exhibition occupies a former educational and spiritual institution dating back to the 15th century. How do you approach a building that already carries such strong narratives before introducing another narrative into it? In most cases where I have designed an exhibition, I’ve had to manage challenging spaces—such as the Hall of Columns at the National Museum of Art of Romania (MNAR) in Bucharest, the Turkish Bath in Iași, and the Știrbei Palace in Bucharest. This project presented another complex layout, yet it was the only time I felt the space could truly harmonise with the exhibition rather than conflict with it. My approach was to strip the space down to its bare essentials, allowing it to host the exhibition without compromising the clarity and integrity of the curatorial discourse or the art itself. I was pleased to design a route that seamlessly connects these distinct, beautiful spaces, highlighting their unique architectural elements like vaults and discreet decorations. Furthermore, specific rooms naturally influenced the arrangement of the artwork, allowing the themes to dialogue directly with the architecture. How do you create a dialogue between a historic building and an artist whose work is itself deeply concerned with memory, time, and continuity? To ensure this connection was established naturally, we sought to neutralise elements that could disrupt the perception of the artwork, such as exposed brick and missing floors. Essentially, we helped the architecture return to its purest form. And since this spatial relationship was inherent from the start, the harmony emerged organically. Since the exhibition opens during Sibiu International Theatre Festival, where audiences are already primed to think theatrically, how do you turn it into an experience that is not passive viewing but active participation? I was influenced by the vision of the curator Liviana Dan who spoke about flight, about immateriality, about Stefan’s solidity as an artist, and about the need for the exhibition to be reduced in expression, as well as her sensitivity to the colours of the building. We arrived at a format that detaches the works from the building itself by exhibiting panels that have a constant geometric shape and that float in the space defined by the walls and massive vaults of the classrooms. We introduced elements that brought a dynamic flow to the perception of the exhibition. They include the vegetable courtyard, which is crossed by a wooden bridge and can signify the passage to another universe; one proposed by the artist, namely the “animal” in the gym class—an oversized exhibition structure that negotiates the relationship between the size of the works and the size of the space; and a new placement of the exhibition panels that contradicts the cartesian shape of the space and introduces dynamics that connect the theme to the performing arts. All this was influenced by the curator’s creative and nonconformist approach. The exhibition title, Transylvania | Extravaganza , suggests something more complex than a geographical region. What kind of Transylvania did you want visitors to encounter: a real place, a cultural memory, or an imagined territory? Honestly, this is a new theme for me, introduced by the curator specifically for this exhibition. I now understand Transylvania to be a fascinatingly complex territory; while situated on the periphery of the empire, its close ties to the imperial centre—manifested through figures like Brukenthal—intertwined with a deep, rural-pastoral and manufacturers’ society. This intersection creates a unique landscape of historical layers that feels multifaceted, as if viewed through a kaleidoscope. Ștefan Câlția has often been described as a “guardian of Transylvania.” How does architecture help translate that idea of stewardship and care into a spatial experience? The Transylvanian territory possesses a powerful identity forged over many centuries. A vital component of this cultural framework—one that inherently shapes the physical landscape—is its architecture in all its diverse forms. Preserving, nurturing, and transmitting these values as they manifest in space, nature, tradition, daily life, and buildings is essential to maintaining this enduring identity. Alongside the exhibition, Ambulanța pentru Monumente is intervening to secure parts of the Ursulines complex and open conversations about heritage preservation. How important was it for you that this project goes beyond displaying art and actively contributes to caring for the building itself? Each project presents a unique opportunity for social dialogue and community activation. The Ambulance for Monuments has intervened to save 100 historical landmarks in just 10 years, making this the perfect moment for an exhibition celebrating the association’s entire trajectory. In the case of the Ursuline Monastery, emergency intervention was vital due to severe roof damage; we know that once water infiltrates a building, degradation accelerates drastically. Revitalising this space and adapting it to seamlessly host cultural and exhibition activities is a major asset for both the city and the community. This achievement was made possible through the collaborative efforts of the Știrbei/Ștefan Câlția Foundation, the Ambulance for Monuments, the Artep Gallery, and all involved sponsors. Is preserving heritage today more about protecting physical structures or about protecting the stories and relationships attached to them? Both tangible and intangible heritages are important, but the principle of “mens sana in corpore sano” applies to architecture as well. Memory is incredibly difficult to safeguard and maintain without physical support—the very body of the building. The better a structure is maintained and cared for, the more vivid the memory and identity of that place remain. Even when a building exists as a ruin, preserving its physical form is vital to keeping its history alive. Is there a particular emotional journey you wanted visitors to experience between entering the building and leaving it? Ultimately, I hope visitors will allow themselves to be carried away by the exhibition, leaving any “baggage” at the entrance to ensure a lighter, more open journey. Transylvania | Extravaganza can be visited at the Ursuline Monastery in Sibiu until 16 August 2026 , daily between 11:00 and 20:00. https://www.dw.com/en/masked-anti-migran.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5LfiT Police said they eventually moved the masked protesters onto trains out of Dover port Image: Oscar Rihll/PA Wire/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Hundreds of masked people blocked traffic at England's port of Dover on Saturday as part of an anti-migrant protest, halting ferry traffic between France and the UK. Video footage showed demonstrators in balaclavas chanting "stop the boats," in a reference to refugees and migrants who attempt the dangerous English channel crossing in a bid to reach Great Britain. This came despite the fact that crossing dropped 40% between January and August 2026 compared to the previous year. However, the perceived threat of migrant boats has become a rallying cry for the far-right Reform UK party. Police said that they were "engaging" with protesters and that normal traffic had resumed at the port after several hours. Government condemns 'travel disruption' "The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but we condemn the behavior in Dover and the travel disruption it has caused," said a spokesman for the government of Prime Minister Andy Burnham. Under Burnham and his predecessor Keir Starmer, migrant crossings have been greatly reduced in part due to closer cooperation with French authorities. Dover is the UK's biggest international ferry port, handling some 15,000 passengers a day during the summer and welcoming more than a third of the UK's trade goods with the European Union. https://telex.hu/gazdasag/2026/09/07/diz.text: Menü Kereső Négy éve nem láttunk ilyen brutális dízelárakat Gazdaság Brückner Gergely Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Tovább emelkednek a hazai üzemanyagárak, de valójában a trend nemzetközi. Itthon a 95-ös benzin literje átlagosan 617 forintba, a gázolajé 697 forintba kerül – írja a Holtankoljak.hu , és mint a Portfolio.hu megjegyezte, utoljára 2022 decemberében voltak ilyen magasan az árak. Az iráni válság során szinte folyamatosan nagyobb volt a termékek áremelkedése, mint magáé az olajé. A Mol Nyrt. részvényei az idén 70 százalékkal drágultak, amit elsősorban a magas finomítói marzsok magyaráznak, de az egész globális dízelpiacra jellemző, hogy a finomítói marzsok nagyon elszálltak. A Baha adatsorai alapján miközben az elmúlt fél évben a brent olaj nagyjából 27 százalékot drágult, addig a dízel 70 százalékot. Az olaj ára cikkünk írása idején 96 dollár/hordó volt, míg a dízelé 1337 dollár/tonna. Ezek eltérő mértékegységek, de a kettőt közös nevezőre hozza az úgynevezett dízel crack spread , amely a finomítók által a nyersolaj dízellé alakításával elért profitmarzsot jelenti. Ez jelenleg 80-85 dollár/hordó, ami kiugróan magas. A szám azt mutatja, hogy egy hordó olaj és egy hordó dízel között mekkora az árkülönbség. Amikor ellátási zavarok vannak, ez az olló nagyon kinyílik, és most sok zavar van. Az ukránok lövik az orosz finomítókat. Emiatt az oroszok nem tudnak, és nem is akarnak annyi dízelt exportálni. A másik nagy exportrégió, vagyis a Közel-Kelet pedig a Hormuzi-szoros válsága miatt nem tudja kihozni a termékeit. Ha a számok mögé nézünk, és 96 dollár egy hordó olaj, és 80-85 dollár a crack spread, akkor kerekítve 175-180 dollárra jön ki egy hordó dízel. Ennek sok különböző benchmarkja van, de Európában az ARA dízelár (ez az Amszterdam, Rotterdam, Antwerpen kikötőire vonatkozó ár) kiemelten fontos. Egy tonna dízel üzemanyag körülbelül 7,3-7,6 hordó, a gázolaj sűrűségétől és a hőmérsékletétől függően az árrésnél átlagosan 7,45-szörös szorzóval kell számolni. Vagyis ha azt látjuk, hogy a dízelár felment 1337 dollár/tonnára, akkor valóban kijön a 179 dollár/hordós dízelár. Dízelkihozatalban amúgy az orosz (Ural vagy REBCO) és az arab könnyű olajtípusok (Arab Light) nagyon kedvezőek. A Reuters szerint a trend folytatódhat. A szezonális kereslet ugyanis az északi féltekén ilyenkor a legmagasabb, hiszen a mezőgazdaságban a betakarítást végző gazdálkodók nagyban dolgoznak, de a déli féltekén is sok a munka, ott a vetésre való felkészülés növeli a dízelfogyasztást az elkövetkező hónapokban. A magasabb dízelárak a tágabb gazdaságra is hatással lehetnek, mivel az üzemanyagot széles körben használják a teherfuvarozásban, a mezőgazdaságban és az iparban, a magas ár növeli a szállítási és termelési költségeket, ami végső soron az élelmiszerárak emelkedéséhez is vezethet. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Andy Burnham has said he is looking at all options for the UK’s relationship with the EU. Photograph: Tobias Schwarz/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham has said he is looking at all options for the UK’s relationship with the EU. Photograph: Tobias Schwarz/AFP/Getty Images Brexit UK could quickly re-enter EU with ‘Switzerland plus’ deal, senior MEP says Bernd Lange, who was involved in Brexit talks, says deal could be negotiated within months of any decision to deepen ties Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent Fri 16 Oct 2026 03.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 16 Oct 2026 06.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK could re-enter the EU in a “Switzerland plus” package that could be negotiated within months of any decision to deepen ties with the bloc, the head of a European parliament committee has said. Bernd Lange, who was heavily involved in Brexit negotiations, said: “I would love to see the UK back.” He said the EU missed the UK in decision-making because of its strong history of promoting open markets and democracy. A Swiss style arrangement is often considered a halfway house to full membership of the bloc but involves free movement and regulatory alignment. View image in fullscreen A Swiss-style relationship with the EU, which is often considered a halfway house to full membership of the bloc, was rejected by the former prime minister Boris Johnson. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA Switzerland is not a member of the EU but it struck a deal last year cementing its “frictionless access” to the single market across more than 100 agreements with a new framework deal. This gives it access to the EU’s electricity market, space programmes, Erasmus and the Digital Europe research programme, and participation in the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. Rejoin, reset or go Swiss-style? How the UK could try to unpick Brexit Read more In exchange, Switzerland agreed to the free movement of people and to pay €375m (£326m) a year into the EU’s economic and cohesion funds. Lange, a German MEP who has an important role in the European legislative process as chair of the European parliament’s trade committee, said the Switzerland framework could be a model for the UK, but it was a “passive” agreement that would not involve the country in EU decision-making. “As a step by step [process], of course, there are a lot of possibilities, but I would love to have the UK come back also in the political decision-making process and politically be engaged. So we have the model of Switzerland … Switzerland plus, I would say, as that has some kinds of engagement but not the full membership.” He said the decision about what relationship the UK wanted with the EU was entirely “in the hands of the UK”, but if it opted for something like Switzerland plus, an agreement could be achieved quickly, notwithstanding political hiccups. He was speaking in London, where his schedule includes a meeting with the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, who is part of a team working on the UK’s new position on EU relations . View image in fullscreen Bernd Lange, the chair of the European parliament’s trade committee, said he supported Andy Burnham’s call for the UK not to be locked out of the EU’s Made in Europe legislation. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP Lange also threw his weight behind Andy Burnham’s call for the EU not to lock the UK out of Made in Europe legislation that would restrict UK suppliers from inclusion in public procurement tenders as well as some corporate contracts such as car fleets. French and German leaders were reportedly close on Thursday to agreeing a proposal that the UK could be included, provided it aligned with the EU’s 2024 tariffs on imports of Chinese electric vehicles. This week the boss of Mercedes said the EU would be making a “deliberate choice” to harm the EU car industry if it did not allow the UK into the Made in Europe package. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Burnham has backing from the Netherlands, Germany and Italy. France, which came up with the legislative proposals, was opposed, saying it needed to get the legislation on the books urgently to guard against cheap competition from China, and that allowing the UK and other allied countries in could hold up the lawmaking. Lange said the UK should “of course” be included because it was already aligned with the EU on environmental standards and employment laws. View image in fullscreen A Mercedes-Benz factory in Germany. The boss of Mercedes this week called for the UK to be included in the Made in Europe package. Photograph: Christoph Steitz/Reuters He said France’s position was “not rational” and “also so emotional” but could be born from the desire to be seen as putting France first before next April’s presidential elections, in which Marine Le Pen, who is opposed to globalism, could take power. Locking the UK out of Made in Europe could also cause a legal dispute over the trade and cooperation agreement that allows UK goods to be sold in the single market without barriers as long as they the meet the bloc’s standards. The Made in Europe package, or the Industrial Accelerator Act, is expected to get political approval by the end of the year or early 2027, meaning Burnham does not have much time to get clauses inserted designating the UK as European for the purposes of the legislation. But Lange said there could be time after that, given the processes of the European parliament, where three committees have scrutinising powers. “There are 5,100 amendments,” he said, referring to the protracted process ahead, including one on UK inclusion. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text: Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog. Donald Trump intensified his anti-Muslim rhetoric against Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed on Sunday, portraying him as a threat to national security. The president also questioned his loyalty to the United States in remarks that drew a sharp rebuke from a former top Arab American ally. Trump called El-Sayed, a former Detroit health official, a “jihadist” who was “on the side of the terrorists” and would “have to go through a metal detector before he’s allowed to go into the Senate.” He also repeatedly invoked 9/11, drawing a comparison between stopping El-Sayed from entering the Senate chamber and the passengers who fought back against the hijackers aboard United Flight 93, AP reported. El-Sayed, who would become the nation’s first Muslim senator if elected, has called attacks on his loyalty to the country “shameful” and repeatedly denied any ties to extremist groups.
